_note: European Portuguese pronunciation drills by first language, for /cultura/erros and the Aussprache-Check. Each drill practises one Portuguese sound or pattern that is hard from a particular first language (transfer, see fehler-nach-sprache.json). `pairs`: minimal pairs, the first word is the target, the second is what often comes out instead or a word to tell it apart from; both are real Portuguese words. `words`: practice words without a partner. `sentence`: to repeat, scored like the Aussprache-Check; it contains one word of every pair. `fehler`: the ids of the mistakes in fehler-nach-sprache.json that this drill practises (the other side of their `drill`; checked by pnpm check:aussprache). European Portuguese (Portugal); the file's `variety` covers every drill, and `ptBR` says where Brazil differs. Drill ids that still fit kept their slot id (aspiration is gone; h, s-z, betonung, doble, enlace, nasal are kept in meaning), the rest are new (content-plan §5.6). Languages: English, German, Spanish, French and Italian speakers; Arabic, Russian, Ukrainian and Chinese drills were removed with the Spanish course and come back only with reliable content. Audio: public/audio/muttersprache/<slug>.mp3 once pt-PT recordings exist; until then the browser voice reads them. Sound descriptions are simplified; to verify with a phonetician or teacher.

ptBR.note: In Brazil unstressed vowels are fuller: pequeno sounds like “pekeno”. The strong reduction is a European Portuguese feature.

reducao.title: Weak vowels: the unstressed e
reducao.tip: In Portugal, vowels that are not stressed become weak and short. An unstressed e is a very short sound or nothing at all: pequeno is nearly “p'keno”, telefone nearly “t'lefon'”. Stress one syllable, and let the others fall away. Don't say every vowel in full.
reducao.sentence: Esta semana estudo português com o meu telefone.

o-u.title: Final o sounds like u
o-u.tip: An unstressed o, above all at the end of a word, sounds like u: livro is “livru”, obrigado is “obrigadu”. Round your lips and keep it short. Don't say a clear Spanish or Italian o.
o-u.sentence: Obrigado, o meu amigo comprou um livro bonito.

aberta-fechada.title: Open and closed: é ê · ó ô
aberta-fechada.tip: é and ó are open: your mouth is wider, like the vowels of “bed” and “not”. ê and ô are closed: round your lips and raise your tongue, like French “thé” and “beau”. Don't glide. A wrong vowel can change the word: avó is grandmother, avô is grandfather.
aberta-fechada.sentence: A minha avó pode ir, mas o meu avô não pôde.

nasal.title: Nasal vowels
nasal.tip: A vowel before m or n at the end of a syllable is nasal: let the air go through your nose, and don't close the sound with a clear m or n. bom is not “bone”, bem is not “bem” with an m. Before a vowel there is no nasal vowel: ano and cama have a clear n and m.
nasal.sentence: Vim comprar lã e vi um bom preço.

ao.title: ão, ãe, õe: nasal diphthongs
ao.tip: Start with the nasal vowel and glide on to a short w (ão) or y (ãe, õe), in one syllable. No clear n at the end. Think “pãw”, “mãy”, “põy”. mão (hand) and mau (bad) are different words, and so are são (they are) and sou (I am).
ao.sentence: Tenho o pão na mão e as laranjas são boas.

ptBR.note: In most of Brazil s before a consonant and at the end of a word is a plain s (mas, festa). In Rio it is sh, as in Portugal.

s-sh.title: s and z as sh
s-sh.tip: In Portugal an s before a consonant or at the end of a word is sh, and a final z too: mas “mash”, festa “feshta”, luz “loosh”. Before b, d, g, m, n, l, r, v it is the s of “measure”: mesmo “mezhmu”. Before a vowel in the next word it is z: os amigos “oz amigos”.
s-sh.sentence: Os meus pais gostam de festas, mas não de peixe.

s-z.title: s between vowels is z; ss and ç are s
s-z.tip: A single s between two vowels buzzes like z: casa, rosa, coisa. ss, ç and c before e or i are a sharp s, as in “sun”: caça, passo, cidade. Put your fingers on your throat: casa shakes, caça doesn't.
s-z.sentence: Em casa, o meu avô assa carne e fala da caça.

ptBR.note: In much of Brazil the strong r is an h-like sound (rato ≈ “hatu”), and r at the end of a word is often said strongly.

r-rr.title: r or rr?
r-rr.tip: A single r between vowels is one quick tap of the tongue tip behind your top teeth. A strong r (at the start of a word, after n, l, s, and rr) is made at the back of your mouth, close to the French r. A final r is weak. caro (expensive) and carro (car) are different words.
r-rr.sentence: O meu carro era caro e eu corro todos os dias.

lh-nh.title: lh and nh
lh-nh.tip: lh and nh are one sound each: press the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. lh is like “million”, nh like “canyon”. Don't say l + y or n + y as two sounds. velho (old) and vela (candle) are different words.
lh-nh.sentence: O velho põe o molho no prato.

j-g.title: j, and g before e or i
j-g.tip: j, and g before e or i, is the s of “measure”: a soft, buzzing sh. It is not the j of “jam”, not a German y and not a Spanish rasp. já (already) and chá (tea) are different words, and so are gelo (ice) and cheio (full).
j-g.sentence: Já tenho gelo e o copo está cheio.

ch.title: ch is sh
ch.tip: ch is sh, as in “shop”. It is not the ch of “church” (English, Spanish), not a German ch and not a k. chave (key) and cave (cellar) are different words.
ch.sentence: A chave está na capa da cave.

doble.title: Short consonants, no double sounds
doble.tip: Italian has long consonants. In Portuguese, rr and ss are written double, but each is one short sound: carro, pessoa, passo. Move straight on to the next vowel. Every other consonant is single.
doble.sentence: A pessoa é bela e fala de tudo.

ptBR.note: In Brazil l at the end of a syllable is like u: Brasil sounds like “Brasiu”. In Portugal it is a dark l.

l-final.title: Dark l at the end of a syllable
l-final.tip: At the end of a syllable l is dark in Portugal: raise the back of your tongue, so that it sounds almost like a short “w”, as in English “full”. It is not a clear Spanish, French or Italian l. Before a vowel l is clear: lua, bola.
l-final.sentence: O hotel azul fica ao sul de Portugal.

h.title: h is silent
h.tip: Never say the letter h at the start of a word: hoje is “oje”. Start straight on the next vowel, and don't breathe out first.
h.sentence: Hoje o homem do hotel tem uma história.

enlace.title: No stop between words
enlace.tip: Don't start a word that begins with a vowel with a small stop in your throat. Let the words run together: os amigos is “oz amigos”, uma hora is “uma ora”, de amigos is nearly “d'amigos”.
enlace.sentence: Os amigos da Ana moram em Évora e ela é de Aveiro.

betonung.title: Stress and written accents
betonung.tip: Every word has one strong syllable, and the written accent shows it when it breaks the rules. An accent can change the word, and the unstressed syllables become weak. Say the stressed syllable longer and clearer.
betonung.sentence: Ontem falámos com a Ana, que está no país com os pais.
